description: The lunge is a unilateral lower-body exercise that develops strength, balance, and coordination in the quads, hamstrings, and glutes independently for each leg. Because each leg works separately, lunges also reveal and correct left-right muscle imbalances. Proper form demands control in two planes simultaneously — forward and vertical.
cues: Stand tall like a soldier — shoulders back, chest open
Step far enough that your front shin stays vertical when you drop down
Drop the back knee straight down — do not let it swing forward
Your front knee tracks over your second toe — not your big toe, not inside it
Drive through the heel of your front foot as you push back up
Keep your hips level — do not let one hip hike up
rules: Keep torso upright throughout the movement
Front knee aligned with second and third toes
Lower back knee toward the ground in a controlled manner
Push through the front heel to return to standing
Maintain balance — do not wobble side to side
Keep hips level — no lateral tilt
constraints: Do not collapse front knee inward (valgus)
Do not lean the torso forward
Avoid shallow lunges — back knee should clear 90 degrees or lower
Avoid using momentum or stepping unevenly
Maintain symmetry between left and right legs

leaning_forward.cause: Tight hip flexors or weak core failing to keep the torso upright under load.
leaning_forward.consequence: Forward lean shifts load onto the lower back and reduces glute activation in the front leg.
leaning_forward.fix: Think of a string pulling the top of your head to the ceiling. Engage your abs. Stretch hip flexors before lunging.

knee_collapse.cause: Weak glute medius or poor neuromuscular control of the knee on the front leg.
knee_collapse.consequence: Medial knee stress — identical risk to squats. A consistent pattern leads to patellar tracking issues.
knee_collapse.fix: Actively press the front knee outward toward your pinky toe. Add lateral band walks to your warmup.

shallow_lunge.cause: Short step length or insufficient hip mobility prevents a deep descent.
shallow_lunge.consequence: Reduced range of motion means less muscle fiber recruitment — you are only getting partial benefit.
shallow_lunge.fix: Take a bigger step forward. The back knee should drop to within 2–3 inches of the floor.

loss_of_balance.cause: Weak stabilisers, particularly the ankle and hip, on the front leg.
loss_of_balance.consequence: Compensatory movements develop and the risk of ankle/knee injury increases.
loss_of_balance.fix: Practice static split squats (stationary lunges) before adding movement. Build single-leg balance training.

using_momentum.cause: Rushing reps or using a bounce at the bottom to initiate the ascent.
using_momentum.consequence: Reduces muscle engagement and adds uncontrolled joint stress at the lowest position.
using_momentum.fix: Hold the bottom position for one second before pressing back up. Think: slow down, power up.

uneven_step.cause: Stepping too short on one side or placing feet on an imaginary tightrope rather than hip-width.
uneven_step.consequence: Asymmetric loading, lateral instability, and reinforcing muscle imbalances.
uneven_step.fix: Step forward so feet remain shoulder-width apart laterally — as if walking on two parallel train tracks, not one rail.

tilt.note: Forward tilt of torso — ideally near zero in a lunge

acceleration.note: Smooth descent and ascent — no bouncing

gyro.note: Lateral sway during lunge step — keep controlled

stability.note: Balance score — single-leg stance is inherently harder

symmetry.note: Compare left vs right leg sensor readings for balance
